title: Organic Reactions: Naming, Ethanol & Polymers
description: Naming organic compounds from their suffixes, making ethanol by fermentation and by catalytic hydration of ethene, ethanol combustion and uses, ethanoic acid as a typical weak acid, and addition polymerisation and the disposal of plastics for IGCSE Chemistry 0620.

notes.heading: Naming Organic Compounds
notes.body:
0620 Core expects you to name and recognise FIVE compounds — methane, ethane, ethene, ethanol and ethanoic acid — and the suffix system behind them.

📌 The suffix tells you the family
• **-ane** = alkane (single bonds only): methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆.
• **-ene** = alkene (contains C=C): ethene C₂H₄.
• **-ol** = alcohol (contains –OH): ethanol C₂H₅OH.
• **-oic acid** = carboxylic acid (contains –COOH): ethanoic acid CH₃COOH.
The stem tells you the number of carbons: meth- = 1, eth- = 2, prop- = 3, but- = 4.

🔑 How it works
Read the name in two parts. 'Ethan-oic acid': eth- means 2 carbons, -oic acid means a –COOH group, so the molecule is CH₃COOH. 'Eth-an-ol': 2 carbons with an –OH group, C₂H₅OH.

💡 Worked Example
A question shows CH₄ and asks for the name. Count the carbons (1 → meth-) and check the bonds (all single → -ane): methane. The same molecule drawn as its displayed formula, with four C–H lines, is still methane.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing ethene with ethane. Both have 2 carbons, but -ene promises a double bond: ethane is C₂H₆, ethene is C₂H₄. Two extra hydrogens is the whole difference.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Stem = carbon count (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-); suffix = family.
• The Core five: methane, ethane, ethene, ethanol, ethanoic acid.

notes.heading: Making Ethanol by Fermentation
notes.body:
Fermentation is the oldest chemical process in the world, and 0620 tests its exact conditions — learn all four.

📌 Definition
Fermentation converts a sugar such as glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide using enzymes in yeast:
**glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide**
C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂

🔑 The four conditions (each is a mark)
1. **Yeast** provides the enzymes that catalyse the reaction.
2. A **sugar (glucose) solution** in water — from fruit, grain or sugar cane.
3. A warm temperature of about **30 °C** — too cold and the enzymes work slowly; too hot and they are denatured.
4. **Anaerobic conditions** (no oxygen) — the mixture is kept away from air, otherwise the ethanol would be oxidised further.

💡 Worked Example
A student ferments glucose solution in a flask fitted with a bubble trap. Bubbles of carbon dioxide escape through the trap while air is kept out. After several days the solution contains a few percent ethanol, which can then be separated by distillation.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying fermentation needs oxygen. Aerobic conditions stop ethanol building up — the process must be anaerobic.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Yeast + sugar solution + about 30 °C + no oxygen.
• Products: ethanol AND carbon dioxide (both appear in the equation).

notes.heading: Making Ethanol from Ethene (Hydration)
notes.body:
Industry can also make ethanol directly from ethene — a completely different route from fermentation.

📌 Definition
In the **catalytic hydration of ethene**, ethene (from the cracking of petroleum fractions) reacts with steam in the presence of a catalyst, at high temperature and pressure:
**ethene + steam → ethanol**
C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH

🔑 How it works
The C=C double bond opens and the elements of water (H and OH) add across it — one carbon gains the H, the other gains the OH. The catalyst speeds the reaction up without being used up, and the process runs continuously in a reactor.

💡 Worked Example
A chemical plant cracks naphtha to obtain ethene, then passes ethene and steam over a hot catalyst. The product stream contains ethanol, which is purified by distillation. Compare with fermentation: same product, completely different raw material (petroleum rather than sugar crops).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing the equation with oxygen: C₂H₄ + O₂. Hydration adds WATER, not oxygen — the only reactants are ethene and steam.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Ethene + steam, catalyst, high temperature and pressure → ethanol.
• The water molecule adds across the C=C double bond.

notes.heading: Ethanol: Combustion and Uses
notes.body:
Ethanol earns its place on the syllabus three ways: as a solvent, as a fuel, and in alcoholic drinks.

📌 Combustion of ethanol
Ethanol burns in a plentiful supply of oxygen with a clean blue flame:
**ethanol + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water**
C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
Because it burns cleanly, ethanol is used as a fuel in its own right — in spirit burners, and blended into petrol (gasohol) in many countries.

📌 Uses (learn all three)
• **Solvent** — ethanol dissolves many substances that do not dissolve in water, so it is used in perfumes, aftershaves, tinctures and marker-pen inks.
• **Fuel** — spirit burners and petrol blends; it can be made from renewable crops.
• **Alcoholic drinks** — the ethanol in beer and wine is made by fermentation.

💡 Worked Example
Balance the combustion equation by counting atoms: 2 C on the left gives 2CO₂; 6 H gives 3H₂O; then count oxygen on the right (4 + 3 = 7), subtract the 1 oxygen already in ethanol, and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 O₂ molecules.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the oxygen atom INSIDE ethanol when balancing. Ethanol is C₂H₆O, so one of the seven oxygens needed is already supplied by the fuel itself.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Complete combustion: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
• Uses: solvent, fuel, drinks.

notes.heading: Ethanoic Acid: A Typical Weak Acid
notes.body:
Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) is the acid in vinegar. It is a WEAK acid, but its reactions are the classic acid reactions you already know — and the exam expects all three.

📌 The three reactions of an acid
1. **With a metal** (such as magnesium): a salt and hydrogen gas form — the metal fizzes and dissolves.
   ethanoic acid + magnesium → magnesium ethanoate + hydrogen
2. **With a base** (a metal oxide or hydroxide, such as copper(II) oxide or sodium hydroxide): a salt and water form.
   ethanoic acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium ethanoate + water
3. **With a carbonate** (such as sodium carbonate): a salt, water and carbon dioxide form — effervescence is the observation.
   ethanoic acid + sodium carbonate → sodium ethanoate + water + carbon dioxide

📌 Naming the salt
Salts of ethanoic acid are called **ethanoates** — the '-oic acid' ending becomes '-oate': sodium ethanoate, magnesium ethanoate. The same rule turns any carboxylic acid into its salt name.

🔑 Weak acid behaviour
Ethanoic acid only partially ionises in water, so it reacts more slowly and has a higher pH than a strong acid of the same concentration — but the PRODUCTS of its reactions are exactly the same as any acid's.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Naming the salt 'sodium ethanoic'. Salts never keep the word 'acid' — ethanoic acid forms ethanoates.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Metals → salt + H₂; bases → salt + H₂O; carbonates → salt + H₂O + CO₂.
• Ethanoic acid → ethanoate salts.

notes.heading: Addition Polymerisation: Ethene to Poly(ethene)
notes.body:
The alkenes made by cracking earn their keep here: they are the monomers for the plastics industry.

📌 Definitions
• A **monomer** is a small, reactive molecule that can join to many others like it.
• A **polymer** is a very long molecule built from thousands of repeating monomer units.
• In **addition polymerisation**, many unsaturated monomers (each containing C=C) join together to form ONE product — the polymer — with nothing left over.

🔑 How it works
Under the right conditions the C=C double bond of each ethene molecule opens up. Each carbon can then bond to a carbon in the next molecule, linking the monomers into a chain. The polymer is named poly(monomer): ethene gives **poly(ethene)** — note the brackets in the name.

💡 Worked Example
Draw the repeat unit of poly(ethene). Start from the monomer CH₂=CH₂: open the double bond to a single bond and give each carbon a free bond pointing outwards: –CH₂–CH₂–. That two-carbon unit, repeated n times, is the polymer chain. Writing the repeat unit with a leftover C=C is the classic error — there are no double bonds left in poly(ethene).

📌 Uses
Poly(ethene) is flexible, waterproof, an electrical insulator and chemically unreactive, so it is used for plastic bags, bottles, food wrap, toys and cable insulation.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing the polymer as (C₂H₄)ₙ with a double bond still in place. Addition polymerisation CONSUMES the double bond — the chain is fully saturated.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Many monomers → one polymer; no other product (that is what 'addition' means).
• Poly(ethene) = ethene monomers with the C=C opened into single bonds.

illustration.alt: Three ethene monomer molecules, each drawn as H2C double-bond CH2, joining by addition polymerisation into a section of a poly(ethene) chain in which the repeat unit of two CH2 groups is shown in brackets with a subscript n.
illustration.caption: Addition polymerisation: the C=C double bonds of many ethene monomers open and link into one saturated chain — poly(ethene).

notes.heading: Plastics and the Environment
notes.body:
The properties that make plastics useful — cheap, strong, unreactive — are exactly what make them hard to throw away. 0620 asks you to discuss the disposal problem, not just name it.

📌 Why disposal is a problem
Addition polymers such as poly(ethene) are **non-biodegradable**: microbes cannot break down their saturated carbon chains, so they do not rot. A plastic bag in landfill can persist unchanged for hundreds of years, and the volume of waste fills landfill sites and pollutes land and oceans.

🔑 The three disposal routes — and their drawbacks
1. **Landfill**: cheap, but the plastic takes up space and never degrades; sites fill up.
2. **Incineration (burning)**: shrinks the waste and can generate energy, but releases carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas) and, for some plastics, toxic gases that must be scrubbed from the flue.
3. **Recycling**: the plastic is sorted, washed, melted and remoulded, conserving the finite petroleum it was made from — but sorting mixed plastics is difficult and costly, so only some plastics are recycled.

💡 Worked Example
A council proposes to burn its plastic waste instead of landfilling it. One advantage: the volume of waste is greatly reduced and energy can be recovered. One disadvantage: burning releases CO₂ and possibly toxic gases, contributing to climate change and air pollution.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that plastics 'cannot be destroyed at all'. They CAN be burned — the problem is the gases released, not indestructibility.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Non-biodegradable → persists in landfill.
• Incineration saves space but pollutes; recycling saves resources but needs sorting.

flashcards.definition: Name ending for an alkane — a hydrocarbon with single C–C bonds only.
flashcards.example: Methane (CH₄) and ethane (C₂H₆) both end in -ane.

flashcards.definition: Name ending for an alkene — a hydrocarbon containing a C=C double bond.
flashcards.example: Ethene, C₂H₄, is the simplest alkene.

flashcards.definition: Name ending for an alcohol — a compound containing the –OH functional group.
flashcards.example: Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, is the alcohol in wine and beer.

flashcards.definition: Name ending for a carboxylic acid — a compound containing the –COOH functional group.
flashcards.example: Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, is the acid in vinegar.

flashcards.definition: The conversion of sugar (glucose) solution into ethanol and carbon dioxide using yeast enzymes at about 30 °C in the absence of oxygen.
The manufacture of ethanol by reacting ethene with steam over a catalyst at high temperature and pressure.
Ethanol is used as a solvent (perfumes, inks), as a fuel (spirit burners, petrol blends) and in alcoholic drinks.
The salt formed when ethanoic acid reacts with a metal, base or carbonate; '-oic acid' becomes '-oate'.
flashcards.example: Ethanoic acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium ethanoate + water.

flashcards.definition: A small reactive molecule that can join to many identical molecules to form a polymer.
flashcards.example: Ethene is the monomer used to make poly(ethene).

flashcards.definition: The joining of many unsaturated monomer molecules (each with C=C) to form a single polymer product, with no other product formed.
flashcards.example: n CH₂=CH₂ → the poly(ethene) chain of –CH₂–CH₂– repeat units.

flashcards.definition: The addition polymer of ethene: a saturated chain of repeating –CH₂–CH₂– units; flexible, waterproof and unreactive.
flashcards.example: Used for plastic bags, bottles, food wrap and cable insulation.

flashcards.definition: Cannot be broken down by microorganisms, so the material persists in the environment for hundreds of years.
flashcards.example: Poly(ethene) bags persist in landfill, which is why recycling and reducing use matter.

questions.stem: What is the name of the compound CH₄?
questions.explanation: One carbon gives the stem meth-, and with only single bonds (no functional group) the suffix is -ane: methane.

questions.stem: A compound's name ends in -ene. What does this tell you about the molecule?
choices: It contains a C=C double bond
questions.explanation: The suffix -ene marks an alkene, whose functional group is the C=C double bond. -ol indicates an alcohol, -oic acid a carboxylic acid, and -ane a fully saturated alkane.

questions.stem: What is the name of the compound C₂H₅OH?
questions.explanation: The stem eth- means two carbons and the –OH group gives the suffix -ol, so C₂H₅OH is ethanol. Ethanoic acid would need the –COOH group (CH₃COOH).

questions.stem: In fermentation, yeast converts glucose into ethanol and which other product?
questions.explanation: The fermentation equation is C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, so carbon dioxide is the other product — the bubbles seen escaping from the fermenting mixture.

questions.stem: Which reactants and conditions are used to manufacture ethanol industrially from ethene?
choices: Ethene and steam, passed over a catalyst
Ethene and oxygen, in bright sunlight
Ethene and hydrogen, with a nickel catalyst
Ethene and bromine water, at room temperature
questions.explanation: Catalytic hydration reacts ethene with steam over a catalyst at high temperature and pressure: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH. Hydrogen with nickel would give ethane, not ethanol.

questions.stem: What are the products when ethanol burns completely in a plentiful supply of oxygen?
questions.explanation: Complete combustion of any fuel containing C and H gives carbon dioxide and water: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. Carbon monoxide appears only when oxygen is limited.

questions.stem: Which list gives three recognised uses of ethanol?
choices: Food preservative, fire extinguisher, anaesthetic gas
questions.explanation: The 0620 list of ethanol uses is: a solvent (perfumes, inks), a fuel (spirit burners, petrol blends) and alcoholic drinks.

questions.stem: Sodium carbonate is added to ethanoic acid. Which gas is produced?
questions.explanation: Ethanoic acid behaves as a typical acid with a carbonate: salt + water + carbon dioxide. The effervescence is CO₂; hydrogen is given off with metals such as magnesium instead.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide. What is the name of the salt formed?
questions.explanation: Salts of ethanoic acid are ethanoates — the '-oic acid' ending becomes '-oate'. The reaction is ethanoic acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium ethanoate + water.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid is described as a TYPICAL weak acid. Which set of observations would you expect when it reacts?
choices: Magnesium gives carbon dioxide; sodium carbonate gives hydrogen
Copper(II) oxide gives oxygen; magnesium gives chlorine
Sodium hydroxide gives only a salt; no water is formed
Magnesium fizzes, giving hydrogen; sodium carbonate effervesces, giving carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Like any acid, ethanoic acid gives salt + hydrogen with metals and salt + water + carbon dioxide with carbonates. 'Weak' describes how fully it ionises, not which products form.

questions.stem: Poly(ethene) is made from which monomer?
questions.explanation: Addition polymerisation needs a monomer with a C=C double bond, and only ethene has one. The polymer name echoes the monomer: ethene → poly(ethene).

choices: Many small unsaturated monomer molecules joining together to form one polymer molecule, with no other product
A polymer breaking down into its monomers when heated
Two different monomers reacting together and losing water
A monomer reacting with oxygen to form a polymer and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation thousands of C=C-containing monomers link into a single chain and nothing else is produced. Losing a small molecule such as water would describe a different type of polymerisation.

questions.stem: What is the repeat unit of poly(ethene)?
questions.explanation: When ethene monomers join, each C=C opens to a single bond, freeing one bond per carbon to link to the next monomer. The repeat unit is therefore –CH₂–CH₂–; a double bond left in the chain is the classic exam error.

questions.stem: Which statement about disposing of poly(ethene) waste is correct?
choices: It biodegrades in landfill within a few weeks
Burning it produces no waste gases
It is non-biodegradable, so it persists in landfill, and burning it can release harmful gases
questions.explanation: Addition polymers have saturated chains that microbes cannot break down, so they persist for hundreds of years in landfill. Incineration reduces the volume but releases CO₂ and, from some plastics, toxic gases — which is why recycling is encouraged.

questions.stem: Balance the complete combustion of ethanol: C₂H₅OH + xO₂ → yCO₂ + zH₂O. What are x, y and z?
questions.explanation: Two carbons give y = 2 CO₂; six hydrogens give z = 3 H₂O. The right side then holds (2 × 2) + 3 = 7 oxygens; one is already inside the ethanol molecule, so 6 more are needed, giving x = 3 O₂: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
